## Statement

Let $N\ge0$ and let $x_0<\cdots<x_{N+1}$ be real nodes. Set
$\omega(t)=\prod_{j=0}^{N+1}(t-x_j)$ and
$w_i=\prod_{j\ne i}(x_i-x_j)$. If $g$ is a real polynomial of degree at most
$N$, then
$$\sum_{i=0}^{N+1}\frac{g(x_i)}{w_i}=0.$$
If, for one fixed $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, the values
$\varepsilon(-1)^i g(x_i)$ are all nonnegative, then $g$ is the zero
polynomial.

1.1 Each $w_i\ne0$. The Lagrange polynomial $L_i(t):=\omega(t)/((t-x_i)w_i)$ has degree $N+1$ and values $L_i(x_j)=1$ for $j=i$ and $0$ otherwise. Thus $H(t):=\sum_i g(x_i)L_i(t)$ has degree at most $N+1$ and agrees with $g$ at all $N+2$ nodes. By [F1], $H-g=0$, so $H=g$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]
cases.reason: At least two strictly ordered interpolation nodes are required even at constant degree, so an empty node list cannot define these weights.

## Definition

Use [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]: each finite
binary coordinate is interpreted as its exact dyadic rational $m2^e$. Write
$\mathbb D=\{m2^e:m,e\in\mathbb Z\}$. All real signs and squared-distance
comparisons use the order of [[def-complete-ordered-real-field]]. For a positive
integer $s\ge1$ and a square matrix $M=(M_{ij})_{0\le i,j<s}$ over $\mathbb D$, define
$$
\det M=\sum_{\pi\in S_s}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_{i=0}^{s-1}M_{i,\pi(i)},
$$
where $S_s$ is the set of permutations of $\{0,\ldots,s-1\}$ and
$\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}$ with
$\operatorname{inv}(\pi)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}$.

For $d\in\{2,3\}$ and ordered points $p_0,\ldots,p_d\in\mathbb D^d$, let
$H_d$ have row $i$ equal to $(p_i,1)$ and put $O_d=\det H_d$. The orientation
predicate returns $\operatorname{sgn}(O_d)\in\{-1,0,+1\}$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}(x)=+1$ for $x>0$, $0$ for $x=0$, and $-1$ for $x<0$. For ordered points
$p_0,\ldots,p_{d+1}$, let $K_d$ have row $i$ equal to
$(p_i,\sum_{j=1}^d p_{i,j}^2,1)$ and put $L_d=\det K_d$. The raw incircle
predicate ($d=2$) or insphere predicate ($d=3$) returns
$\operatorname{sgn}(L_d)$; its zero is an exact determinant zero. The row order
is the point order displayed, and the column order is the coordinate columns,
then squared norm, then $1$. If $O_d\ne0$, define the orientation-normalized
side sign algebraically to be $\operatorname{sgn}(O_dL_d)$. Whenever a sphere
through $p_0,\ldots,p_d$ is specified, positive means inside it, zero means on
it, and negative means outside. If
$O_d=0$, the base simplex is degenerate and only the raw lifted determinant
sign is specified.

An uncertain coordinate input is a real interval with finite dyadic endpoints,
as defined in [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]]. Its values remain
uncertain throughout a certified computation; a midpoint is not substituted.
For real $c\in\mathbb R^d$ and $r\ge0$, write
$S(c,r)=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\sum_j(x_j-c_j)^2=r^2\}$; inside, on, and outside
mean that this squared distance is less than, equal to, or greater than $r^2$.
cases.reason: The determinant expansion is restricted to positive matrix order, so the empty permutation-product convention is never required here.

binary coordinate is interpreted as its exact dyadic rational $m2^e$. Write
$\mathbb D=\{m2^e:m,e\in\mathbb Z\}$. All real signs and squared-distance
comparisons use the order of [[def-complete-ordered-real-field]]. For a positive

$$

$\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)=(-1)^{\operatorname{inv}(\pi)}$ with
$\operatorname{inv}(\pi)=\#\{(i,j):i<j,\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}$.

$\operatorname{sgn}(L_d)$; its zero is an exact determinant zero. The row order

sign is specified.

## Definition

For a finite index set $E$ and a complex array $z=(z_e)_{e\in E}$, define
$$\|z\|_1=\sum_{e\in E}|z_e|,\qquad \|z\|_2=\left(\sum_{e\in E}|z_e|^2\right)^{1/2},\qquad \|z\|_\infty=\max_{e\in E}|z_e|.$$
For $z,w\in\mathbb C^E$, define the counting inner product by $\langle z,w\rangle_E=\sum_{e\in E}z_e\overline{w_e}$. By [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], $\langle z,z\rangle_E=\sum_{e\in E}|z_e|^2$, so $\|z\|_2=\sqrt{\langle z,z\rangle_E}$. For $E=\varnothing$, all three norms and this inner product are defined to be zero. For nonempty finite $E$, the maximum exists by repeated comparison in the real order. Complex modulus is as in [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]], conjugation as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]], and the square root is the unique nonnegative root.

1.1 For $E=\varnothing$ all three values are stipulated as zero. If $E$ is nonempty finite, enumerate its elements and induct on the number of entries. A one-entry list of real moduli has a maximum; given a maximum for the first $n$ entries, compare it with the $(n+1)$st modulus using [F2] and [F4] and keep the larger. Induction [F5] constructs the maximum of the finite modulus list. The finite sum formulas in [F1] are well-defined. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, induction]

## Statement

Let $M\in\mathbb F^{p\times q}$ be any finite real or complex matrix, and let $M^\dagger$ be its unique Moore-Penrose inverse. Then $P=MM^\dagger$ and $Q=M^\dagger M$ are self-adjoint idempotents. The range of $P$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$, and the range of $Q$ is $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$. Thus both are orthogonal projections. If $M$ has full row rank, then $MM^\dagger=I_p$.

2.1 The range of $P$ is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}(M)$ because $P=MM^\dagger$, while $PM=M$ by [F1], so $\operatorname{Ran}(M)\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}(P)$. Thus $\operatorname{Ran}(P)=\operatorname{Ran}(M)$. The range of $Q$ is contained in $\operatorname{Ran}(M^\dagger)$, and $QM^\dagger=M^\dagger$ by [F1], so these ranges are equal. [F1, step 1.1]
cases.reason: Projection identities concern finite matrices and their ranges; no interpolation interval or parameter endpoint enters the Penrose equations.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V,Q$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $b:V\times Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Define $B:V\to Q$ by $(Bv,q)_Q=b(v,q)$. If $Q=\{0\}$, the unique zero map is a bounded right inverse. If $Q\ne\{0\}$, assume $V\ne\{0\}$ and define
$$\beta:=\inf_{q\ne0}\sup_{v\ne0}\frac{b(v,q)}{\|v\|_V\|q\|_Q}.$$
When $\beta>0$, $B$ is onto and has a bounded linear right inverse $R:Q\to V$ with $BR=I_Q$ and $\|R\|\le\beta^{-1}$.

3.1 Set $Rg:=B^*q$, with $q$ from step 2.1. Uniqueness in Lax–Milgram makes this assignment linear, and the adjoint identity in [F3] gives $BRg=g$. Also $\|Rg\|^2=(g,q)\le\|g\|\|q\|$ while step 2.1 gives $\beta\|q\|\le\|Rg\|$. If $Rg=0$ the desired bound is immediate; otherwise combine and divide to obtain $\|Rg\|\le\beta^{-1}\|g\|$. Thus $R$ is the claimed bounded right inverse. [A1, F2, F3, algebra, step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron with a matching shape-regular affine tetrahedral mesh $\mathcal T_h$. There are a positive continuous piecewise affine function $g_h$, a smooth bounded vector field $b$ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega$, and positive constants $c,C,r,\epsilon_0$, independent of the mesh, with the following properties. On $K$, $c h_K\le g_h\le C h_K$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(g_h)\le C$, where $h_K=\operatorname{diam}K$. Put
$$F_{t,y}^{\pm}(x)=x+t g_h(x)(\pm b(x)+r y),\qquad |y|\le1,\quad 0<t\le\epsilon_0.$$
The maps are uniformly bi-Lipschitz on their domain. For the plus sign, $F_{t,y}^{+}(\overline\Omega)\subset\Omega$. For the minus sign, $F_{t,y}^{-}(\partial\Omega)\subset\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline\Omega$, at distance at least $ctg_h(x)$ from $\partial\Omega$. The same interior distance lower bound holds for the plus sign at boundary points. The images of $K$ and all homotopies $s\mapsto F_{st,y}^{\pm}(x)$, $x\in K$, lie within distance $Ct h_K$ of $K$. Their intersections with $\Omega$ are contained in a vertex patch $\omega_K$ of uniformly bounded overlap, after decreasing $\epsilon_0$ if necessary. All constants may depend on $\Omega$ and the shape-regularity bound. No ratio of global maximum to minimum mesh size occurs.

1.1 Fix the shape-regularity bound $\sigma$. For a cell $K$, let $F_K(\hat x)=b_K+A_K\hat x$ be its orientation-preserving map from the reference tetrahedron. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally a Lipschitz graph, with $D$ on one side in each chart. It need not be connected. There is one linear operator $E:H^1(D)\to H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with $Ef=f$ almost everywhere on $D$, which maps $H^2(D)$ boundedly into $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Its support can be confined to a fixed bounded neighborhood of $\overline D$. The bounds depend only on a finite choice of boundary charts and cutoffs. In particular no mesh enters them.

9.1 For bounded $D$, cover its compact boundary by finitely many graph charts and choose smooth cutoffs supported strictly inside them, together with an interior cutoff, summing to one near $\overline D$. Each localized function is extended by zero within its special graph outside its original chart; since its cutoff vanishes near the chart sides, this is an $H^m$ function on the graph with the expected product derivatives. Apply the graph operator, then multiply the result by a second fixed cutoff supported in the chart and equal to one on the first cutoff's support. On $D$ the result is the localized original function, including the part where that function is zero. The interior term is extended by zero, with no interface near its support. Summing these finitely many extensions gives $E$, preserves the restriction identity, and gives both asserted boundedness estimates by the weak product rule. A final cutoff equal to one near $\overline D$ confines support. Finite graph covers work equally for disconnected $D$; no connectivity or topology is used. All construction coefficients are fixed independently of $f$. This proves the statement. [F3, step 8.1, construct, F4] ∎

At each exterior point the active cube sizes are comparable to $d$, so $c d\le\rho\le Cd$. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^3$ be bounded and Lebesgue measurable, and choose a half-open cube $Q$ of positive side length containing $D$. Subdivide $Q$ into its nested dyadic cubes at mesh $h_N=2^{-N}\operatorname{side}(Q)$. Let $E_{N,j}=D\cap Q_{N,j}$ range over the finitely many cells of positive measure, let $V_N\subset L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ be the functions constant on each such cell, and define $P_N$ by replacing a function on each $E_{N,j}$ by its cell average. Then $P_N$ is the orthogonal projection onto $V_N$, $\|P_N\|\le1$, the spaces $V_N$ are increasing, and $P_Nv\to v$ in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ for every $v\in L^2(D;\mathbb C)$.

1.1 For each positive-measure cell $E_{N,j}$ the average is finite by Cauchy–Schwarz, since $\int_{E_{N,j}}|v|\le |E_{N,j}|^{1/2}\|v\|_{L^2(E_{N,j})}$. For every function constant on the cells, the integral of $v-P_Nv$ against that function is zero cell by cell. Thus $v-P_Nv\perp V_N$ and $P_Nv\in V_N$, so $P_N$ is the orthogonal projection. Pythagoras gives $\|P_Nv\|_2\le\|v\|_2$. [given, F2, construct, algebra]

Pulling them back to $Q$ and restricting to $D$ preserves convergence up to the fixed affine measure factor. Every finite family of base-2 boxes is constant on the cells of a sufficiently fine common dyadic partition, so the restrictions belong to some $V_N$. Thus $\bigcup_NV_N$ is dense in $L^2(D;\mathbb C)$; the partitions are nested, so $V_N\subseteq V_{N+1}$. [F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

## Definition

Fix $d\ge2$ and a bounded connected polyhedral open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$. For each mesh parameter $h$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching shape-regular affine simplicial mesh in the sense of [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], and put $h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K$. Let $V_h$ be the space of continuous functions on $\overline\Omega$ that are affine on every cell and vanish on $\partial\Omega$.

Let $\epsilon>0$, $b\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $c\in C(\overline\Omega)$, and $f\in C(\overline\Omega)$. Define $B:=\|b\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$ and $C:=\|c\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)}$. Assume a fixed $\omega>0$ satisfies $c-\frac12\nabla\cdot b\ge\omega$ on $\Omega$. The boundary condition for this branch is $u=0$ on the whole boundary, including the inflow part $\{x\in\partial\Omega:b(x)\cdot n(x)<0\}$. A classical exact solution is a function $u\in C^2(\overline\Omega)$ satisfying $-\epsilon\Delta u+b\cdot\nabla u+cu=f$ in $\Omega$ and this boundary condition.
cases.reason: The maximum cell diameter and affine finite-element space presuppose a finite mesh covering the specified connected polyhedral open domain.

## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and the unit cell $Y=(0,1)^d$ with Lebesgue measure $|Y|=1$. Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ conventions of [[def-countable-choice]]. A **uniformly elliptic periodic scalar diffusion coefficient** is a measurable real function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ such that $a(y+k)=a(y)$ for almost every $y$ and every $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and there are constants $0<\lambda\le\Lambda<\infty$ with $\lambda\le a(y)\le\Lambda$ almost everywhere on $Y$. Coefficients are identified when they agree almost everywhere.

For $\epsilon>0$, the physical scalar coefficient is $a_\epsilon(x)=a(x/\epsilon)$ and the associated matrix is $a_\epsilon(x)I_d$. The bounded-domain branch used on this page is $\Omega=(0,1)^d$ with homogeneous zero boundary values. Its weak equation for datum $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is
$$\int_\Omega a(x/\epsilon)\nabla u_\epsilon\cdot\nabla v\,dx=\int_\Omega fv\,dx\qquad(v\in H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb R)).$$
No coefficient regularity beyond measurability and the displayed bounds is part of this definition.

For every $\epsilon>0$, the map $x\mapsto x/\epsilon$ is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^d$. By [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]], its pullback preserves Lebesgue measurability and takes null-set changes to null-set changes (apply the theorem also to the inverse map). Thus $a_\epsilon$ is a well-defined almost-everywhere class independent of the representative of $a$. The same result applies to every affine translation and positive dilation used in periodic sampling below, so almost-everywhere coefficient bounds are preserved under those pullbacks.

The ellipticity bounds hold almost everywhere on all of $\mathbb R^d$, not just on $Y$: periodicity transfers the exceptional null set from $Y$ to each lattice translate, translations preserve null sets by the same change-of-variables theorem, and the countably many translates cover $\mathbb R^d$ up to their null boundaries.
cases.reason: The prescribed unit cube has positive measure in positive dimension, and the spatial branch is this cube rather than an arbitrary empty domain.

## Statement

Let $S$ be the closed reference triangle $\overline T$, where $T=\{x,y>0,x+y<1\}$, or the closed interval $[0,1]$, and let $f:S\to\mathbb R$ be real-valued. Write $\mathbb P_p(S)$ for restrictions of real polynomials of total degree at most $p$ on the triangle and degree at most $p$ on the interval. Say that $f$ is smooth up to $S$ when every partial derivative on the interior has a continuous extension to $S$. Suppose that for some $M>0$ and $A\ge1$,

$$
\|D^\alpha f\|_{L^\infty(S)}\le M A^{|\alpha|}|\alpha|!\qquad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha.
$$

Use $\|g\|_{W^{1,\infty}(S)}:=\|g\|_{L^\infty(S)}+\sum_{i=1}^{\dim S}\|\partial_i g\|_{L^\infty(S)}$. Then constants $C,b>0$, depending only on $A$ and the fixed reference domain, satisfy

$$
\inf_{q\in\mathbb P_p(S)}\|f-q\|_{W^{1,\infty}(S)}\le CM e^{-bp}\qquad(p\ge1).
$$

For the interval branch there is also an endpoint-preserving polynomial $J_pf\in\mathbb P_p([0,1])$ whose derivative is the $L^2$ orthogonal projection of $f'$ onto $\mathbb P_{p-1}$. It satisfies $\|(J_pf)'\|_2\le\|f'\|_2$ and $\|f-J_pf\|_{H^1}\le CM e^{-bp}$ after changing $C,b$ by constants depending only on $A$.

5.1 On the interval let $P$ be the $L^2$ orthogonal projection of $f'$ onto $\mathbb P_{p-1}$ and put $J_pf(t)=f(0)+\int_0^tP(s)ds$. The positive-definite finite polynomial Gram matrix gives a unique projection; Pythagoras gives $\|P\|_2\le\|f'\|_2$ and $\|f'-P\|_2\le\|f'-r\|_2$ for every $r\in\mathbb P_{p-1}$. Orthogonality to constants gives $\int_0^1P=\int_0^1f'$, and [F4] evaluates the latter as $f(1)-f(0)$. Thus $J_pf(1)=f(0)+\int_0^1P=f(1)$, while $J_pf(0)=f(0)$ by construction. The derivatives of $f'$ satisfy a factorial bound with fixed constants $M'=MA$ and $A'=2A$, since $(j+1)!\le2^j j!$ for $j\ge1$. For $p\ge2$, apply step 4.1 to $f'$ with degree $p-1$; best approximation of the $L^2$ projection then gives $\|f'-P\|_2\le CMe^{-b(p-1)}$, which is at most $C'Me^{-b'p}$ after changing constants. For $p=1$, the derivative contraction and the bound $\|f'\|_2\le MA$ give the same asserted estimate after enlarging $C'$. Finally $f-J_pf=\int_0^t(f'-P)$ and [F2] bounds its $L^2$ norm by $\|f'-P\|_2$. The derivative and value bounds prove the stated interval estimate. [F2, F4, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be an admitted domain of [[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]], let $X\subset\Omega$ be finite and nonempty, and put $h=h_X$. $$|y_j-x|\le Rh,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^J|\lambda_j|\le B,\qquad p(x)=\sum_{j=1}^J\lambda_jp(y_j)\quad(p\in\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)).$$
No lower bound on site separation is assumed.

3.1 Choose $L>1/\varepsilon$ and set $h_0\le r_0/L$. For the fixed $x$, use [F1] to choose $Q_x$. The normalized points $z'_j=(Lh)^{-1}Q_x^{-1}(y_j-x)$ then satisfy $|z'_j-z_j|\le1/L<\varepsilon$; hence they are distinct and their evaluation weights have sum at most $B$. 1.1 The evaluations at points of the open unit cone $C=\{z:0<|z|<1,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}$ span the dual of $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. Indeed, if fewer than $J$ independent evaluations have been chosen, the map from $\Pi_{m-1}$ to their finite value list has nonzero kernel by [F3]; choose a nonzero polynomial $p$ in that kernel. Since $C$ is nonempty and open (it contains $e_1/2$), it contains a box $I_1\times\cdots\times I_d$ of nonempty open intervals. Write $p$ as a polynomial in its first coordinate, of degree at most $m-1$. For every fixed tuple of the other coordinates in their intervals, this univariate polynomial vanishes at the $m$ distinct points $a_1+\frac{k}{m+1}(b_1-a_1)$, $1\le k\le m$, where $I_1=(a_1,b_1)$. These points lie in $I_1$ by [F4], so the root bound [F2] forces every coefficient to vanish at that tuple. Applying the same argument inductively to each coefficient polynomial on $I_2\times\cdots\times I_d$ shows every coefficient is identically zero, contrary to the choice of $p$. Thus $p$ is nonzero at some point of $C$, and evaluation there increases the independent list. After the finite number $J$ of steps, choose $z_1,\ldots,z_J\in C$ with invertible evaluation matrix. ## Statement

Let $a=x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_m=b$, $m\ge1$, let $y_0,\ldots,y_m\in\mathbb R$,
and let $\sigma_a,\sigma_b\in\mathbb R$. Put
$h_i=x_{i+1}-x_i>0$ and $d_i=(y_{i+1}-y_i)/h_i$. There is exactly one
clamped cubic spline interpolant in the sense of
[[def-clamped-cubic-spline-interpolant]]. Its nodal second derivatives
$M_i=s''(x_i)$ are the unique solution of
$$\begin{aligned}2h_0M_0+h_0M_1&=6(d_0-\sigma_a),\\h_{i-1}M_{i-1}+2(h_{i-1}+h_i)M_i+h_iM_{i+1}&=6(d_i-d_{i-1}),\quad 1\le i<m,\\h_{m-1}M_{m-1}+2h_{m-1}M_m&=6(\sigma_b-d_{m-1}).\end{aligned}$$
On $[x_i,x_{i+1}]$ the interpolant is
$$s_i(x)=\frac{M_i(x_{i+1}-x)^3+M_{i+1}(x-x_i)^3}{6h_i}+\left(y_i-\frac{M_ih_i^2}{6}\right)\frac{x_{i+1}-x}{h_i}+\left(y_{i+1}-\frac{M_{i+1}h_i^2}{6}\right)\frac{x-x_i}{h_i}.$$

3.1 For any clamped interpolant, its nodal second derivatives must satisfy the displayed system by the same endpoint-slope formulas, so invertibility from step 1.1 forces them to equal the constructed $M_i$. On each interval, the difference from $s_i$ is a cubic with zero endpoint values and zero endpoint second derivatives. Its second derivative is affine and vanishes at both endpoints, hence is identically zero; the difference is then affine and vanishes at both endpoint values, hence is zero. Every piece is therefore unique, proving uniqueness of the interpolant. [A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

$$p(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1.$$

If $\lambda\ne0$, then $P(x_i)=-(-1)^i\lambda$ are nonzero alternating values, so $P$ is nonzero and [F1] rules this out. Thus $\ker T=\{(0,0)\}$. [given, F1, F3, F4, F5, construct]

## Statement

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $m,n\ge1$, have a singular value decomposition
$$ A=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*,\qquad \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q>0, $$
where $q=\operatorname{rank}(A)$. For an integer $k\ge0$, put
$$ A_k=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,q)}\sigma_j u_jv_j^*, \qquad \delta_k^2=\sum_{j=k+1}^{q}\sigma_j^2 $$
with an empty sum equal to zero. Then $\operatorname{rank}(A_k)\le k$, $\|A-A_k\|_F=\delta_k$, and every matrix $B$ with $\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k$ satisfies $\|A-B\|_F\ge\delta_k$.

1.1 Choose the full output singular-vector basis $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ from an SVD of $A$, ordered so its first $q$ vectors correspond to the positive singular values in the statement. The SVD sends each positive input singular vector to a nonzero multiple of its corresponding output vector and sends every remaining input basis vector to zero. Thus the image of $A$ is exactly $\operatorname{span}(u_1,\ldots,u_q)$, so $q=\operatorname{rank}(A)$ by [F1]. If $k\ge q$, then $A_k=A$ and $\delta_k=0$, so the lower bound follows from nonnegativity of the norm. Suppose henceforth that $k<q$, and let $B$ have rank at most $k$. Its column image has an orthonormal basis; let $P$ be the orthogonal projection onto that image. Then $PB=B$, and the columnwise orthogonal decomposition by $P$ and $I-P$ gives $\|A-B\|_F^2\ge\|(I-P)(A-B)\|_F^2=\|(I-P)A\|_F^2$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]
cases.evidence: A zero-rank matrix has an empty positive-singular-value list, and both the truncation and its tail error are explicitly zero.

For a finite quadtree and a nonempty root pair as in [[def-finite-planar-quadtree-fmm-pair-lists]], the recursive interaction decomposition terminates. ## Example

Use binary floating-point arithmetic with precision $p=24$, round-to-nearest
ties-to-even, and a normal exponent range containing the values below. Let
$$c=1-2^{-24},\qquad P^-=\begin{bmatrix}1&c\\c&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad H=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad R=2^{-22}.$$
Compute $B= P^-H^T$, then $S=HB+R$, then $K=B/S$, and finally
$P_{\rm sub}=P^- - (KS)K^T$, rounding every displayed operation in the
specified format.

3.1 The computed gain is $K=(1/2,1/2)^T$. Multiplication gives $(KS)K^T=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$ exactly, so the rounded subtractive update is $$P_{\rm sub}= \begin{bmatrix}0&-2^{-24}\\-2^{-24}&0\end{bmatrix}.$$ Its eigenvalues are $2^{-24}$ and $-2^{-24}$, so it is indefinite. This shows cancellation can lose positive semidefiniteness even with an exact positive-definite prior and positive measurement variance. By contrast, when the factor procedure succeeds, [F3] gives a represented covariance that is an exact factor product; this example makes no claim that rounding a later materialization of that product preserves the property. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
cases.reason: The witness prescribes a two-coordinate covariance and a single scalar measurement, so empty state or measurement arrays are outside this example.

## Definition

For real $x>0$, define
$\operatorname{erfcx}(x)=e^{x^2}\operatorname{erfc}(x)$. For each integer
$k\ge0$, define the finite positive moment

$$M_k(x)=\int_0^\infty t^k e^{-t^2-2xt}\,dt.$$

The moments are auxiliary quantities for a finite-depth interval enclosure of
$\operatorname{erfcx}$. They are not the modified Bessel functions $I_k$.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For $\gamma>-1$, define $g_\gamma(0)=0$ and $g_\gamma(x)=x^\gamma$ for $0<x\le1$. Then $g_\gamma$ is Lebesgue measurable and integrable on $[0,1]$, with
$$\int_{[0,1]}g_\gamma\,d\lambda=\frac{1}{\gamma+1}.$$

1.1 For each integer $n\ge1$, define $g_n(x)=x^\gamma$ on $[1/n,1]$ and $g_n(x)=0$ on $[0,1/n)$. For every real $c$, its strict superlevel is all of $[0,1]$ if $c<0$, and $[1/n,1]\cap\{x>0:x^\gamma>c\}$ if $c\ge0$. The latter is Borel because the power is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ by [F4]; hence [F2] makes $g_n$ measurable, and $g_n\ge0$. It is bounded and continuous on each side of its only possible jump at $1/n$; isolating that point in an interval of arbitrarily small length and using uniform continuity on the two remaining compact pieces makes its Darboux gap arbitrarily small, so [F6] gives Riemann integrability. [given, A1, F2, F4, F6, construct]
cases.reason: The integration domain is the prescribed closed unit interval of positive measure; no varying empty measurable domain is under consideration.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For $\gamma>-1$, define $g_\gamma(0)=0$ and $g_\gamma(x)=x^\gamma$ for $0<x\le1$. Then $g_\gamma$ is Lebesgue measurable and integrable on $[0,1]$, with
$$\int_{[0,1]}g_\gamma\,d\lambda=\frac{1}{\gamma+1}.$$

1.1 For each integer $n\ge1$, define $g_n(x)=x^\gamma$ on $[1/n,1]$ and $g_n(x)=0$ on $[0,1/n)$. For every real $c$, its strict superlevel is all of $[0,1]$ if $c<0$, and $[1/n,1]\cap\{x>0:x^\gamma>c\}$ if $c\ge0$. The latter is Borel because the power is continuous on $(0,\infty)$ by [F4]; hence [F2] makes $g_n$ measurable, and $g_n\ge0$. It is bounded and continuous on each side of its only possible jump at $1/n$; isolating that point in an interval of arbitrarily small length and using uniform continuity on the two remaining compact pieces makes its Darboux gap arbitrarily small, so [F6] gives Riemann integrability. [given, A1, F2, F4, F6, construct]
cases.reason: The lemma proves integrability and its value for a specified exponent range; it does not state the converse threshold theorem.

## Statement

Let $f:G\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^3$ and let $\bar u\in G$ be a state at which
$A(\bar u)=Df(\bar u)$ has distinct real eigenvalues
$\lambda_1^0<\cdots<\lambda_m^0$. For each $i$, there is a neighborhood $N_i$
of $\bar u$ and $C^2$ functions $\lambda_i:N_i\to\mathbb R$ and
$r_i:N_i\to\mathbb R^m$ such that $A(u)r_i(u)=\lambda_i(u)r_i(u)$,
$\lambda_i(\bar u)=\lambda_i^0$, and the eigenvectors can be normalized by a
fixed linear functional. After intersecting these finitely many neighborhoods,
the eigenvalues remain real, simple, and ordered, and $r_1(u),\ldots,r_m(u)$
form a basis at each $u$.

3.1 Since $F_i$ is $C^2$, [F2] gives a local $C^1$ eigenpair. The derivative formula in [F2] is $C^1$ because $DF_i$ is $C^1$ and matrix inversion is smooth on invertible matrices; hence the eigenpair is $C^2$. Continuity preserves the eigenvalue gaps and reality after shrinking the neighborhood. [step 2.1, F1, F2]
cases.reason: A base state in the open flux domain is specified, and each eigenpair neighborhood contains that state before their finite intersection.

## Statement

Let $h>0$, $\Delta t\ge0$, $a\in\mathbb R$, and $\mu=|a|\Delta t/h$. Use the direct reconstructed-upwind forward-Euler update for scalar linear advection from [[def-na-high-resolution-reconstruction]], with the stated MUSCL/minmod reconstruction and no time predictor; write $U^+$ for the sequence after one such update. The data are either a real bi-infinite sequence with finite discrete total variation
$$\operatorname{TV}(U)=\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z}|U_i-U_{i-1}|<\infty,$$
or a real $N$-periodic sequence, for an integer $N\ge1$, with
$$\operatorname{TV}_N(U)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}|U_i-U_{i-1}|,$$
where periodic indices are taken modulo $N$. If $0\le\mu\le2/3$, one update satisfies $\operatorname{TV}(U^+)\le\operatorname{TV}(U)$ in the bi-infinite case and $\operatorname{TV}_N(U^+)\le\operatorname{TV}_N(U)$ in the periodic case.

The constant $2/3$ is sharp within the original range $0\le\mu\le1$: for every $2/3<\mu\le1$ there are finite-support data of variation $2$ whose updated variation is $3\mu>2$. For every period $N\ge7$, the same witness periodized with period $N$ has the same strict increase.

2.1 Subtract the identity for $U_{i-1}^+$ in step 1.1 from that for $U_i^+$ to obtain $d_i^+=(1-C_i)d_i+C_{i-1}d_{i-1}$. The coefficients are nonnegative, so $|d_i^+|\le(1-C_i)|d_i|+C_{i-1}|d_{i-1}|$. For periodic data, $C_i$ is $N$-periodic because it is defined from shifts of $U$; summing over one period and cyclically reindexing gives $\operatorname{TV}_N(U^+)\le\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}[(1-C_i)+C_i]|d_i|=\operatorname{TV}_N(U)$. This also covers $N=1$, when every $d_i=0$. For bi-infinite data, both nonnegative series on the right are bounded by $\sum_i|d_i|<\infty$. Reindexing the absolutely convergent second series gives $\operatorname{TV}(U^+)\le\sum_i[(1-C_i)+C_i]|d_i|=\operatorname{TV}(U)$, so the updated sequence still has finite variation. [step 1.1, algebra]
cases.reason: Periodic data have a strictly positive period and bi-infinite data are indexed by all integers; a finite-support witness still has an inhabited ambient grid.

## Statement

Let $(V,H,J)$ be a Banach evolution triple, let $T>0$, and fix
$0\ne v\in V$. For each positive integer $n$, define
$$u_n(t)=\sin(2\pi nt/T)\,v.$$
Then $(u_n)$ is bounded in $L^p(0,T;V)$ for every $1\le p<\infty$, but it
has no strongly convergent subsequence in $L^2(0,T;H)$. Its time-derivative
norm grows linearly in $n$ in every $L^q(0,T;V^*)$, $1\le q\le\infty$.

1.1 Since each interval $[0,T]$ contains exactly $n$ periods of $\sin(2\pi nt/T)$, a change of variable gives $$\|u_n\|_{L^p(0,T;V)}^p =\|v\|_V^p\frac{T}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}|\sin s|^p\,ds,$$ independent of $n$. Thus the family is uniformly bounded in each stated $L^p(V)$. [given, algebra]
cases.reason: The witness fixes a nonzero spatial vector and a positive-length time interval, so neither an empty evolution triple nor an empty observation interval is admitted.

## Statement

Let $(V,H,J)$ be a Banach evolution triple, let $T>0$, and fix
$0\ne v\in V$. For each positive integer $n$, define
$$u_n(t)=\sin(2\pi nt/T)\,v.$$

2.1 The weak derivative is $u_n'(t)=(2\pi n/T)\cos(2\pi nt/T)\,Jv$. Its $L^q(V^*)$ norm is $$(2\pi n/T)\|Jv\|_{V^*} \left(\frac{T}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos s|^q\,ds\right)^{1/q}$$ for finite $q$, and $(2\pi n/T)\|Jv\|_{V^*}$ for $q=\infty$. Since $Jv\ne0$ by [F1], these norms grow linearly in $n$. Hence no positive exponent derivative bound is present. [F1, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $(V,H,J)$ be a Banach evolution triple, let $T>0$, and fix
$0\ne v\in V$. For each positive integer $n$, define
$$u_n(t)=\sin(2\pi nt/T)\,v.$$
Then $(u_n)$ is bounded in $L^p(0,T;V)$ for every $1\le p<\infty$, but it
has no strongly convergent subsequence in $L^2(0,T;H)$. Its time-derivative
norm grows linearly in $n$ in every $L^q(0,T;V^*)$, $1\le q\le\infty$.

1.2 For distinct positive integers $n\ne m$, sine orthogonality over $[0,T]$ gives $$\|u_n-u_m\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}^2 =\|iv\|_H^2\int_0^T (\sin(2\pi nt/T)-\sin(2\pi mt/T))^2\,dt =T\|iv\|_H^2>0,$$ where positivity follows from injectivity in [F1]. Every two distinct members therefore stay a fixed positive distance apart, so no subsequence is Cauchy and none converges strongly in the complete space $L^2(0,T;H)$. [F1, given, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]], let $1<p<\infty$, and suppose
$u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ with distributional derivative

## Statement

Consider one exact-branch two-grid cycle from [[alg-fas-two-grid-cycle]]. Let
$F_h:U_h\to\mathbb R^{n_h}$ and $F_H:U_H\to\mathbb R^{n_H}$ be $C^1$ on
open sets, let $I,R,P$ be linear, and suppose $F_h(u_*)=f_h$ and
$Iu_*\in U_H$. Assume the exact coarse solver selects the local root branch
through $Iu_*$ and $DF_H(Iu_*)$ is invertible. Suppose the pre/post smoothing
maps are $C^1$ and fix $u_*$. The selected coarse root $v(u)$ is locally $C^1$,
and the derivative of the actual FAS cycle $E$ at $u_*$ is
$$DE(u_*)=DS^{\rm post}(u_*)\bigl[I_{n_h}-P\,DF_H(Iu_*)^{-1}R\,DF_h(u_*)\bigr]DS^{\rm pre}(u_*).$$

No identity between $R$ and $I$, or between the coarse operator and a
rediscretized fine operator, is assumed in this derivative formula.

1.1 Define $G(u,v):=F_H(v)-F_H(Iu)-R(f_h-F_h(u))$ on the open product domain where its terms are defined. The given fine root gives $G(u_*,Iu_*)=0$. Since $I$ and $R$ are linear and $F_h,F_H$ are $C^1$, $G$ is $C^1$; its partial derivatives at $(u_*,Iu_*)$ are $D_vG=DF_H(Iu_*)$ and $D_uG=-DF_H(Iu_*)I+RDF_h(u_*)$. The first is invertible by hypothesis. [given, F1, construct, algebra]
cases.reason: A selected coarse root through the restricted fine solution is prescribed, so an empty root branch cannot meet the implicit-function hypotheses.

## Definition

Fix d,N≥1, positive masses m_1,…,m_N, ε>0, the kernel W_ε from [[def-scaled-symmetric-compact-kernel-family]], and a pressure map P∈C¹((0,∞)×R,R). Positions q_i and velocities v_i lie in R^d with the Euclidean inner product from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and specific internal energies e_i lie in R. Define

$$\rho_i(q)=\sum_{j=1}^Nm_jW_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad p_i=P(\rho_i,e_i),\qquad A_i=\frac{p_i}{\rho_i^2}.$$

The state domain is U={ (q,v,e): ρ_i(q)>0 for every i }. On U, the fixed-width semidiscrete system is

$$\dot q_i=v_i,\qquad \dot v_i=-\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(A_i+A_j)\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j),\qquad \dot e_i=A_i\sum_{j=1}^Nm_j(v_i-v_j)\cdot\nabla W_\varepsilon(q_i-q_j).$$

A controlled tube is a compact subset of U on which ρ_i≥ρ_*>0 for every i. The system is semidiscrete: time remains continuous while the spatial state is represented by finitely many particles. It has fixed masses and fixed ε, includes the displayed matched internal-energy equation, and contains no artificial viscosity. No continuum Euler convergence is part of this definition.

For every continuous kernel $k$ on $[0,1]^2$, the composite midpoint Nyström
operators $K_N$ converge to the integral operator $K$ in the operator norm on

## Definition

For each $i$, let $W_i$ be the vector space of local boundary nodal traces compatible with the fixed outer Dirichlet values, and set $W=\prod_i W_i$ (all interface copies independent). Let $\widehat W\subset W$ be the subspace whose nodal traces agree at every shared interface node; let $R:\widehat W\to W$ be the inclusion. Choose a set of **primal constraints**, meaning finitely many linear functionals on local traces whose values are required to agree across their incident subdomains. Vertex values and normalized edge averages are examples. The **partially assembled space** $\widetilde W$ is the subspace of $W$ satisfying those primal equalities, so $\widehat W\subset\widetilde W\subset W$.

The remaining continuity equations are collected in a jump map $B:\widetilde W\to\mathbb R^m$ with $\ker B=\widehat W$. It may contain redundant rows. Fix the **redundant-multiplier convention** $\Lambda:=\operatorname{range}B$ with its inherited Euclidean inner product: multiplier vectors are elements of this range, not arbitrary row-coordinate vectors modulo an unstated choice. Then $B^T$ is injective on $\Lambda$. For the PE26 two-dimensional estimate, all subdomain vertices are primal and the only remaining jump rows are nodal differences on open interface edges, each shared by exactly two subdomains.

An interface corner is primal whenever its value is among the selected primal functionals. An **edge average** on a side $E$ is $|E|^{-1}\int_E v_h\,ds$, which is a finite sum of nodal values for a $P_1$ trace. The two-dimensional bound below uses corner constraints; no edge-average bound is claimed there.
cases.evidence: With no remaining jump rows, the multiplier range is the zero-dimensional space and injectivity of the transpose there is vacuous.

## Definition

For each $i$, let $W_i$ be the vector space of local boundary nodal traces compatible with the fixed outer Dirichlet values, and set $W=\prod_i W_i$ (all interface copies independent). Let $\widehat W\subset W$ be the subspace whose nodal traces agree at every shared interface node; let $R:\widehat W\to W$ be the inclusion. Choose a set of **primal constraints**, meaning finitely many linear functionals on local traces whose values are required to agree across their incident subdomains. Vertex values and normalized edge averages are examples. The **partially assembled space** $\widetilde W$ is the subspace of $W$ satisfying those primal equalities, so $\widehat W\subset\widetilde W\subset W$.

The remaining continuity equations are collected in a jump map $B:\widetilde W\to\mathbb R^m$ with $\ker B=\widehat W$. It may contain redundant rows. Fix the **redundant-multiplier convention** $\Lambda:=\operatorname{range}B$ with its inherited Euclidean inner product: multiplier vectors are elements of this range, not arbitrary row-coordinate vectors modulo an unstated choice. Then $B^T$ is injective on $\Lambda$. For the PE26 two-dimensional estimate, all subdomain vertices are primal and the only remaining jump rows are nodal differences on open interface edges, each shared by exactly two subdomains.

An interface corner is primal whenever its value is among the selected primal functionals. An **edge average** on a side $E$ is $|E|^{-1}\int_E v_h\,ds$, which is a finite sum of nodal values for a $P_1$ trace. ## Statement

Let $Y=(0,1)^d$ and $V_\#$ be the mean-zero periodic $H^1$ space of [[def-periodic-zero-mean-cell-space]]. Then every $v\in V_\#$ satisfies
$$\|v\|_{L^2(Y)}\le\sqrt d\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(Y)},$$
and every $v\in H^1_\#(Y)$ satisfies $\int_Y\nabla v=0$. Consequently $\|\nabla v\|_2$ is a complete norm on $V_\#$ equivalent to its inherited $H^1$ norm.

1.2 For smooth periodic $v$, write $m=\int_Yv(y)\,dy$. For $x,y\in Y$, telescope from $y$ to $x$ one coordinate at a time. The $i$th difference is the integral of $\partial_i v$ along a segment of length at most one, with the earlier coordinates fixed at $x$ and later coordinates fixed at $y$. Cauchy--Schwarz [F3] bounds its square by the integral of $|\partial_i v|^2$ along the full unit coordinate interval. The inequality $|\sum_{i=1}^d b_i|^2\le d\sum_i|b_i|^2$ and Tonelli [F4], integrating in $x$ and $y$, then give $\int_Y\int_Y|v(x)-v(y)|^2\,dy\,dx\le d\sum_{i=1}^d\|\partial_i v\|_2^2.$ For each $x$, Jensen's inequality gives $|v(x)-m|^2=|\int_Y(v(x)-v(y))dy|^2\le\int_Y|v(x)-v(y)|^2dy$. Integrating in $x$ proves the stated inequality for smooth periodic mean-zero $v$. [F3, F4, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T=\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0,\ x+y<1\}$, let $r\ge5$ be an integer, let $p\ge2r-4$ be an integer, and put $n=\lfloor p/2\rfloor$ and

$$
\eta_{n,r}=\left(\frac{(n-r+3)!}{(n+r-5)!}\right)^{1/2}.
$$

There is a bounded linear map $A_{p,r}:H^r(T;\mathbb R)\to\mathbb P_p(T;\mathbb R)$, where $\mathbb P_p(T;\mathbb R)$ is the restriction of real polynomials in $(x,y)$ of total degree at most $p$. It is explicitly defined in the proof from the reference-simplex extension, a unique moment polynomial, and finite Legendre projections, and satisfies

$$
\|u-A_{p,r}u\|_{H^2(T)}\le C_r\eta_{n,r}|u|_{H^r(T)}.
$$

Here $C_r$ is independent of $p$ and is the product of a fixed reference extension bound, the reference moment-projection bound, and an absolute tensor-projection constant; no useful growth bound in $r$ is asserted. For a shape-regular affine triangle $K$ of diameter $h_K$, affine transport gives

$$
\left(\sum_{j=0}^2h_K^{2j-2}|u-A_{K,p,r}u|_{H^j(K)}^2\right)^{1/2}\le C_{r,\gamma}\eta_{n,r}h_K^{r-1}|u|_{H^r(K)}.
$$

If $p\ge4(r-2)$, then $\eta_{n,r}\le(4/p)^{r-4}$. This is a conservative ordinary Sobolev rate; it is neither an optimal $p^{-(r-1)}$ estimate nor an analytic growth estimate for $C_r$.

1.1 On $I=(-1,1)$ define $S_nf(x)=f(-1)+(x+1)f'(-1)+\int_{-1}^x(x-t)\Pi_{n-2}f''(t)\,dt,$ where $\Pi_{n-2}$ is the ordinary Legendre $L^2$ projection. Here $p\ge2r-4$ implies $n\ge r-2\ge3$. For $f\in H^2(I)$, the endpoint values are those of its absolutely continuous representatives from [F4]. The polynomial $S_nf$ has degree at most $n$ and matches $f,f'$ at $-1$. Its second derivative is an $L^2$ contraction; integrating twice and using the one-dimensional endpoint estimate gives $\|S_nf\|_{H^2(I)}\le C\|f\|_{H^2(I)}$ with absolute $C$. For every integer $s\ge3$ with $n\ge s-1$, the error $e=f-S_nf$ has $e(-1)=e'(-1)=0$ and $e''=f''-\Pi_{n-2}f''$. Apply the Legendre tail estimate to $f''$ with derivative order $s-2$ and projection degree $n-2$; the factorial ratio is $\rho_{n,s}=\left(\frac{(n-s+1)!}{(n+s-3)!}\right)^{1/2}.$ Two integrations of $e''$, with Cauchy–Schwarz [F5], give $\|e\|_{H^2(I)}\le C\rho_{n,s}\|f^{(s)}\|_2$. The same inequality holds for each derivative of order at most two. [A1, F1, F4, F5, given, construct, algebra]

## Statement

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge1$, and $d\in\mathbb N$ with $d<n$; let
$x_0<\cdots<x_n$, and let $x$ be distinct from these nodes. For every
$0\le i<n-d$, put
$$G_i:=f[x_i,\ldots,x_{i+d},x].$$
Then
$$G_i-G_{i+1} =-(x_{i+d+1}-x_i)f[x_i,\ldots,x_{i+d+1},x].$$

1.1 Apply the recursive endpoint rule [F1] to the order-$(d+2)$ divided difference on the ordered endpoints $x_i,x_{i+d+1}$ and the intermediate list $x_{i+1},\ldots,x_{i+d},x$. Symmetry [F2] identifies its two numerator terms as $G_{i+1}$ and $G_i$, respectively, so $$f[x_i,\ldots,x_{i+d+1},x] =\frac{G_{i+1}-G_i}{x_{i+d+1}-x_i}.$$ [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

## Statement

Let $M=\sum_s U_sV_s^*$ be the finite matrix input to [[alg-hlr-core-svd-recompression-with-tolerance]], and let $k$ and $\delta\ge0$ be its rank cap and Frobenius tolerance. If the algorithm returns **success** with rank $q$, its returned matrix $\widehat M$ has rank $q$ and satisfies $\|M-\widehat M\|_F=(\sum_{j>q}s_j(M)^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. No lower-rank matrix meets the same tolerance. If the algorithm returns **tolerance-not-met**, no matrix of rank at most $k$ meets the tolerance.

2.1 On success, the output factors in [F1] form the rank-$q$ truncation of the lifted SVD in step 1.1. Its retained singular values are positive and their singular vectors are orthonormal, so its rank is exactly $q$. Applying [F4] gives $\|M-\widehat M\|_F=(\sum_{j>q}s_j(M)^2)^{1/2}\le\delta$. By the minimal choice in [F1], every smaller $r<q$ has discarded tail greater than $\delta$; [F4] then rules out every rank-at-most-$r$ approximation meeting the tolerance. If the algorithm fails, then $k<t$ and the tail at $k$ is greater than $\delta$ (otherwise $q=k$ would pass); [F4] rules out every rank-at-most-$k$ approximation. This includes $q=0$, $k=0$, zero factors, and repeated singular values. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: A zero represented factor sum has no positive core singular values, so rank zero succeeds with zero tail and no missing SVD vector.

## Statement

The map $G$ defined in [[def-godunov-flux-for-burgers]] is continuous on
$\mathbb R^2$ and satisfies $G(a,a)=f_B(a)=a^2/2$ for every $a\in\mathbb R$.

2.1 At a boundary with $a=b>0$ both adjacent formulas tend to $a^2/2$; at $a=b<0$ both tend to $a^2/2$; at $a=0\le b$ the left and right limits are zero; at $a\le0=b$ the limits are zero. On the remaining axis portions $a=0>b$ and $b=0<a$, a neighborhood lies in the single shock branch $b<a$, whose formula is continuous there. At $(a,b)=(0,0)$ every branch has absolute value at most $\max\{a^2,b^2\}/2$, which tends to zero. These checks cover every branch boundary and prove continuity on all of $\mathbb R^2$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

## Definition

Let $d\ge2$, let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite matching affine simplicial mesh whose boundary faces are paired by translations to form a periodic mesh, let $V_K=\int_K1\,dx$ be cell volume, and let $A_F=\int_F1\,dS$ be face area. Let $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ be constant, and let $U_K\in\mathbb R$ be one cell mean per cell. For each face $F\subset\partial K$, let $n_{K,F}$ be the outward unit normal, $b_{K,F}=\beta\cdot n_{K,F}$, and $K_F$ the neighboring cell across that periodic face. With $b^+=\max(b,0)$ and $b^- =\min(b,0)$, the upwind flux out of $K$ is
$$\widehat f_{K,F}=b_{K,F}^+U_K+b_{K,F}^-U_{K_F}.$$
For a step $\Delta t>0$, first compute
$$\lambda_K=\frac{\Delta t}{V_K}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}A_Fb_{K,F}^+.$$
The **degree-zero upwind forward-Euler update** is admissible when $\lambda_K\le1$ for every cell; its output is
$$U_K^+=U_K-\frac{\Delta t}{V_K}\sum_{F\subset\partial K}A_F\widehat f_{K,F}.$$
This is the degree-zero specialization of [[def-pe04-upwind-dg-transport-discretization]].
cases.reason: The algorithm divides by each positive simplex volume and takes a maximum of cellwise admissibility conditions, so an empty geometric mesh is not supplied.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $d_k,\tau_k>0$ tend to zero, set $I_i^k=[id_k,(i+1)d_k)$, $x_i^k=(i+\tfrac12)d_k$, $t_n^k=n\tau_k$, and $J_n^k=[t_n^k,t_{n+1}^k)$, and let $b\in C^1(\mathbb R)$ be locally Lipschitz. On each cell-time slab let $h_k,u_k$ be piecewise constant, with $h_k\ge0$, $u_k=0$ when $h_k=0$, and $m_k=h_ku_k$. Suppose $h_k\to h$ and $u_k\to u$ strongly in $L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$, $u=0$ almost everywhere where $h=0$, and $h_k,|u_k|$ are locally uniformly bounded. Let $\mathcal F_k(x,t)=\widehat F_{i+1/2}^{k,n}$ for $(x,t)\in I_i^k\times J_n^k$, with face flux from [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]] and bed samples $b(x_i^k)$. Then
$$\mathcal F_k\longrightarrow F(h,hu)\quad\text{strongly in }L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R\times(0,T)).$$
The primitive-velocity convergence and uniform velocity bound are included because the assigned wave-speed formula uses $m/h$ on wet states, which is not continuous at a dry state as a function of $(h,m)$ alone.

1.1 Fix a compact space-time rectangle $Q$ and a fixed compact enlargement $Q'$ containing $Q$ and every spatial translate $Q+d_k$ for all sufficiently large $k$. Choose local bounds $H,M$ so that $0\le h_k\le H$ and $|u_k|\le M$ on $Q'$. Strong local $L^1$ convergence implies the same bounds for $h,u$ almost everywhere on $Q'$: the sum $|h_k-h|+|u_k-u|$ tends to zero in $L^1(Q')$, so [F4] gives a subsequence on which both converge almost everywhere and inherit the bounds. By [F3], multiplying $h,u$ by the indicator of $Q'$ therefore gives $L^1(\mathbb R^2)$ functions. The given strong convergence gives $h_k\to h$ and $u_k\to u$ in $L^1(Q)$. Applying [F2] to the cutoffs shows $h(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to h$ and $u(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to u$ in $L^1(Q)$. Strong local convergence on $Q'$ and the triangle inequality then show $h_k(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to h$ and $u_k(\cdot+d_k,\cdot)\to u$ in $L^1(Q)$ as well. [A1, F2, F3, F4, given, algebra]

## Statement

For two compatible conforming NVB descendants $\mathcal T_1,\mathcal T_2$ of the same initial mesh $\mathcal T_0$, the union of their bisection forests defines a smallest common conforming overlay $\mathcal T_1\oplus\mathcal T_2$ and
$$\#(\mathcal T_1\oplus\mathcal T_2)\le\#\mathcal T_1+\#\mathcal T_2-\#\mathcal T_0.$$

1.1 Let $F_i$ be the finite binary forest for $\mathcal T_i$. Their node union $F=F_1\cup F_2$ is a forest: every nonroot node keeps its parent, and a node is either a leaf in both forests or has its same two children in at least one; if it has children in either forest, the union contains both. The common initial edges have equal labels. Induct on the bisection depth of any shared edge: its midpoint is uniquely determined by the segment, and its two half-edge labels are determined by the same generation rule [F1]; therefore both incident forests prescribe the same descendants on that edge. The leaves of $F$ consequently form a matching conforming triangulation refining both $\mathcal T_1$ and $\mathcal T_2$. Any common refinement must contain every node split in either forest, so it contains $F$ and refines its leaf partition. Thus this is the smallest common conforming overlay. [F1, given, construct]

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, as in the Sobolev trace and inverse-estimate suppliers.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a conforming shape-regular triangular mesh, let $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solve the model of [[def-afem-p1-residual-estimator-and-data-oscillation]], and let $U\in V(\mathcal T)$ be its exact P1 Galerkin solution. There are constants $C_{\rm rel},C_{\rm eff}$ depending only on the shape bound and $|b|h_{\max}$ such that
$$\|\nabla(u-U)\|_2^2\le C_{\rm rel}\eta(U,\mathcal T)^2,$$
and for every $K\in\mathcal T$,
$$\eta_K(U)^2\le C_{\rm eff}\left(\|\nabla(u-U)\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}^2+ \operatorname{osc}(U,\omega_K)^2\right),$$
where $\omega_K$ is the union of $K$ and its edge neighbors. If $\mathcal T_*\ge\mathcal T$ refines every cell in $M\subset\mathcal T$ by three generations and $U_*$ is the exact fine Galerkin solution, then
$$\eta(U,\ M)^2\le C_{\rm eff}\left(\|\nabla(U_*-U)\|_{L^2(\omega(M))}^2+ \operatorname{osc}(U,\omega(M))^2\right),$$
with $\omega(M)$ the union of edge-neighbor patches of marked cells. All constants are independent of the refinement level.

3.1 For the marked correction set $d=U_*-U$. On each marked cell and each of its edges use the same fine bubble tests as in steps 1.2 and 2.1. For any such test $v_*$, fine Galerkin orthogonality gives $a(u-U_*,v_*)=0$, so the coarse residual functional on $v_*$ equals $a(d,v_*)$. Write $\omega=\operatorname{supp}v_*$ and $h_\omega=\operatorname{diam}\omega$. The convection vector $b$ is constant by the model definition. Since the cell or edge bubble $v_*$ vanishes on $\partial\omega$, its local Poincare inequality gives $\|v_*\|_{L^2(\omega)}\le Ch_\omega\|
abla v_*\|_{L^2(\omega)}$. Consequently the original form, without transferring a derivative to the bubble, satisfies $|a(d,v_*)|\le\|
abla d\|_{L^2(\omega)}\|
abla v_*\|_{L^2(\omega)}+|b|\|
abla d\|_{L^2(\omega)}\|v_*\|_{L^2(\omega)}\le C(1+|b|h_\omega)\|
abla d\|_{L^2(\omega)}\|
abla v_*\|_{L^2(\omega)}$. Thus no zero trace or zero patch mean of $d$ is assumed. The cell-data remainder is exactly the stated oscillation. Since each bubble vanishes on the patch boundary, its local Poincare inequality bounds its $L^2$ norm by the patch diameter times its gradient norm. The bubble scaling from steps 1.2 and 2.1 therefore bounds every marked contribution by the correction plus oscillation; bounded overlap proves the displayed marked estimate. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

On the same periodic Q1/Q1 mesh and with the same checkerboard pressure from [[ex-supg-q1-equal-order-pressure-checkerboard]], add any grad-div coefficient $\gamma\ge0$ to the velocity equation but omit PSPG. The pressure mode remains a nonzero null vector for every $\gamma$.

## Statement

Let $d=1$ and let $A_t$ be an ALE moving-domain map of [[def-ale-moving-domain-map]], so $\widehat\Omega$ is a finite union of bounded intervals with pairwise disjoint closures and $\partial_\xi A_t>0$. For every $C^1$ scalar field $g$ on the moving closure,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega(t)}g(x,t)\,dx=\int_{\Omega(t)}\partial_tg(x,t)\,dx+\sum_{x\in\partial\Omega(t)}g(x,t)w_m(x,t)n(x),$$

where $n=-1$ at each left endpoint and $n=+1$ at each right endpoint. This dimension-one branch is choice-free.

2.1 For any continuous $h$ on $K_t$, its zero extensions from $\Omega(t)$ and $K_t$ to a nondegenerate closed interval containing $K_t$ in its interior are bounded and can be discontinuous only at $B_t$. By [F11] they are integrable. Their difference is supported on $B_t$ and bounded in absolute value by a constant times $1_{B_t}$; [F8] gives $\int 1_{B_t}=0$, so [F7] shows their integrals agree. The same argument applies on $\widehat K$ and $\widehat\Omega$. The map image in [F3] is compact Jordan, and [F5] makes $g(\cdot,t)$ and $G(\cdot,t)$ integrable on the compact closures. Change of variables on those closures, followed by the open/closed equalities just proved, gives $I(t)=\int_{\widehat K}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi=\int_{\widehat\Omega}G(\xi,t)\,d\xi$, where $G(\xi,t):=g(A_t(\xi),t)J(\xi,t)$. [F3, F5, F7, F8, F11, step 1.1, algebra]

## Example

For $H>0$, interpolate $f(x)=x^2$ naturally at $0,H,2H$. The error on the
first interval is $H^2/16$ at its midpoint, even though $f^{(4)}=0$. The
clamped interpolant with exact endpoint slopes is $f$ itself. This displays
why the fourth-order bound for the clamped method requires compatible
boundary data.

3.1 Since $f^{(4)}=0$, a general natural-boundary estimate of the form $C H^4\|f^{(4)}\|_\infty$ would force zero error, contradicting step 2.1. The polynomial $f$ has the prescribed clamped slopes $f'(0)=0$ and $f'(2H)=4H$, so [F2] makes it the unique clamped interpolant; [F3] also gives zero error. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{n_1\times\cdots\times n_d}$ and let $\widehat A$ be the truncated HOSVD with mode-rank caps $r_1,\ldots,r_d$. Then
$$ \|A-\widehat A\|_F \le \sqrt d\inf_{B\in\mathcal T_r}\|A-B\|_F, $$
where $\mathcal T_r$ is the set of tensors whose $k$th unfolding has rank at most $r_k$.

1.1 Let $P_k=U_kU_k^*$ be the orthogonal projection used in mode $k$, and let $\mathcal P_k$ denote its action on that mode. The projections $\mathcal P_k$ commute for distinct modes, since they act on different tensor indices. By [F4], $\widehat A=\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_dA$. The telescoping identity gives $A-\widehat A=\sum_{k=1}^d\mathcal P_1\cdots\mathcal P_{k-1}(I-\mathcal P_k)A$. For $k<\ell$, the $k$th summand lies in the kernel of $\mathcal P_k$, while the $\ell$th lies in its range. These summands are orthogonal, so their squared norms add. [F4, F5, algebra]
cases.reason: Commuting orthogonal mode projections give a quasioptimal error bound, without characterizing every tensor that attains the best multilinear rank error.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, let $0\le d<n$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and fix a real query point
$x\in[x_0,x_n]$ distinct from the nodes. Let $f\in C^{d+1}([x_0,x_n])$, put
$g=f^{(d+1)}$, and suppose $g$ has finite total variation
$V=\operatorname{Var}_{[x_0,x_n]}(g)$ as defined in
[[def-bounded-variation-and-total-variation]]. For $0\le i\le n-d$, put
$G_i=f[x_i,\ldots,x_{i+d},x]$. Then
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n-d-1}|G_{i+1}-G_i|\le \frac{V}{(d+1)!}.$$

1.1 By [F4], $d+1\in\mathbb N$, so apply [F1] to each $G_i$, using the same simplex coordinates for each window and using the final coordinate for the fixed point $x$. Thus $$G_i=\int_{\Delta_{d+1}}g(y_i(u))\,du,\qquad y_i(u)=u_xx+\sum_{k=0}^{d}u_kx_{i+k},$$ where all coefficients are nonnegative and sum to one. By [F3], $g$ is continuous on the closed interval. Therefore every $y_i(u)$ lies in $[x_0,x_n]$. [given, F1, F3, F4, construct]
cases.reason: At least two ordered nodes and an interior distinct query point are prescribed, so there is always an inhabited list of divided-difference windows.

## Statement

Let $n\ge0$ be an integer, $x\ge0$, $m\ge1$, $h=\pi/m$, and
$$f(\theta)=e^{-x(1-\cos\theta)}\cos(n\theta),\qquad Q_m=h\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}f((j+1/2)h).$$
Then
$$\left|e^{-x}I_n(x)-\frac{Q_m}{\pi}\right| \le \frac{h^2}{24}\bigl((x+n)^2+x\bigr).$$
The bound certifies the exact midpoint integral. Floating-point summation is
certified only if its operations are enclosed separately.

1.1 Put $g(\theta)=e^{-x(1-\cos\theta)}$. Since $1-\cos\theta\ge0$, we have $0<g\le1$ on $[0,\pi]$. Differentiation gives $g'=-x\sin\theta\,g$ and $g''=(-x\cos\theta+x^2\sin^2\theta)g$. Thus $|g'|\le x$ and $|g''|\le x+x^2$. For $f=g\cos(n\theta)$, $$|f''|\le |g''|+2n|g'|+n^2|g| \le x+x^2+2nx+n^2=(x+n)^2+x.$$ [given, L9, algebra]

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $T>0$, $f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, $u_0\in L^\infty(\mathbb R)\cap L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)$, and $F\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be continuous with $F(a,a)=f(a)$ for every $a\in\mathbb R$. For each $m$, form the conservative finite-volume scheme and space-time reconstruction of [[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]] and [[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]] using $h_m,\tau_m\to0$ and initial cell averages of $u_0$. Suppose reconstructions converge strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$ to $u$, and for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is $M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on $I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is a locally bounded distributional weak solution in the sense of [[def-locally-bounded-distributional-weak-solution]]; explicitly, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times(-\infty,T))$,
$$
\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\bigl(u\varphi_t+f(u)\varphi_x\bigr)\,dx\,dt +\int_{\mathbb R}u_0(x)\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.
$$
The strong convergence and local uniform bounds are hypotheses, not conclusions. No CFL condition or entropy inequality is assumed, so the theorem proves a weak limit only; it does not claim Kruzhkov entropy admissibility. If the limit is also globally essentially bounded, this identity is the published bounded weak formulation in [[def-distributional-weak-solution-of-a-scalar-conservation-law]].

2.3 For each $j,n$, translation of a cell interval and the fundamental theorem of calculus give $\tau_m(\Phi_{j+1}^{m,n}-\Phi_j^{m,n}) =\int_{J_n^m}\int_{I_j^m}\frac1{h_m}\int_0^{h_m}\varphi_x(x+s,t)\,ds\,dx\,dt$. Its difference from $\int_{J_n^m}\int_{I_j^m}\varphi_x$ is at most $C_\varphi h_m^2\tau_m$, by the bound on $\varphi_{xx}$. The numerical face fluxes are uniformly bounded on cells meeting the test support because $F$ is continuous on the compact state square supplied by local boundedness. Summing over the finitely many cells and time slabs meeting the test support gives total error $O(h_m)$. Thus the flux sum in [F3] differs from $\int_0^T\int\mathcal Q_m\varphi_x$ by a quantity tending to zero. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]
cases.reason: The reconstruction is on the real line over a strictly positive time interval, while compact test support merely makes its local sums finite.

## Statement

For every finite measure $\mu$ on a bounded nondegenerate interval or nondegenerate affine simplex $K$ that assigns positive measure to every nonempty relatively open subset, every $p\ge0$, and every $u\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, the set $\mathcal P_K(u)$ in [[def-pe04-cellwise-l2-projection]] contains exactly one polynomial $\Pi_Ku$. For each $w\in\mathbb P_p(K)$,
$$\|u-\Pi_Ku\|_{L^2(K)}\le\|u-w\|_{L^2(K)}.$$

1.1 Choose the finite monomial basis $\{\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_M\}$ of $\mathbb P_p(K)$. Its Gram matrix $G_{ij}=\int_K\phi_i\phi_j\,d\mu$ is positive definite: for every nonzero coefficient vector $c$, the polynomial $q=\sum_i c_i\phi_i$ is continuous and nonzero at some point of $K$, so it is bounded away from zero on a nonempty relatively open subset; full support gives $c^TGc=\int_Kq^2\,d\mu>0$. Each moment $b_i=\int_Ku\phi_i\,d\mu$ is finite by [F2]. The invertible system $Gc=b$ therefore has a unique solution, and $p=\sum_i c_i\phi_i$ satisfies [F1]. [F1, F2, construct, algebra]

## Statement

Let $u$ be a classical solution of $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $r>a$, where $k>0$, and satisfy the outgoing condition in [[def-pe18-exterior-helmholtz-problem]]. For each $\ell$, its orthogonal projection $u_\ell(r,\cdot)$ onto $\mathcal H_\ell$ has the form $u_\ell(r,\cdot)=c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ with a fixed vector $c_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Before imposing outgoingness, every degree-$\ell$ coefficient is a linear combination of $h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ and $h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)=\overline{h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)}$. This statement is modewise; it does not assert convergence of the partial-wave series as $r\to\infty$.

1.1 Fix $\ell$ and any $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$. Define $w_v(r)=\langle u(r,\cdot),v\rangle_{L^2(\mathbb S^2)}$. Integrating the polar-coordinate Helmholtz equation against $v$, using $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v=-\ell(\ell+1)v$ and the angular integration-by-parts identity from [F2], gives $w_v''+2r^{-1}w_v'+(k^2-\ell(\ell+1)r^{-2})w_v=0$. Since this holds for every vector in the finite-dimensional space, the projected vector $u_\ell(r,\cdot)$ solves the same scalar radial equation componentwise. [F1, F2, algebra]
cases.reason: A classical outgoing field is defined on the nonempty exterior radial region, while every harmonic degree is treated by its finite-dimensional projection.

## Statement

Let $u$ be a classical solution of $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ for $r>a$, where $k>0$, and satisfy the outgoing condition in [[def-pe18-exterior-helmholtz-problem]]. For each $\ell$, its orthogonal projection $u_\ell(r,\cdot)$ onto $\mathcal H_\ell$ has the form $u_\ell(r,\cdot)=c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ with a fixed vector $c_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. This statement is modewise; it does not assert convergence of the partial-wave series as $r\to\infty$.

2.1 Apply the uniform radiation condition [F1] to any $v\in\mathcal H_\ell$ and integrate it against $\bar v$; its coefficient tends to zero because its magnitude is bounded by the uniform supremum times $\|v\|_{L^1}$. For the outgoing mode, the asymptotic and derivative recurrence in [F3] give $r(\partial_r-ik)h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)\to0$. For the incoming conjugate, the same recurrence gives $r(\partial_r-ik)h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)=-2i\,\overline{(-i)^{\ell+1}}e^{-ikr}+o(1)$, whose magnitude tends to $2$. Thus its coefficient in the mode combination from step 1.2 must vanish. Since this holds for every $v$, the projected vector is $c_\ell h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ for a fixed $c_\ell\in\mathcal H_\ell$. The argument treats each degree separately and uses no interchange of the degree sum with the limit $r\to\infty$. [F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

1.2 The two functions $h_\ell^{(1)}(kr)$ and $h_\ell^{(2)}(kr)$ solve this equation and have nonzero Wronskian by [F3]–[F4]; hence at any fixed $r_0>a$ their value-derivative vectors form an invertible $2\times2$ matrix. Solve this matrix equation to match a coefficient and its derivative at $r_0$. The difference then solves a first-order system $Y'=M(r)Y$ with continuous $M$ and zero initial data. On each compact interval where $\|M\|\le C$, integration gives $|Y(r)|\le C\int_{r_0}^r|Y(s)|ds$ (or the reversed integral for $r<r_0$); Grönwall's inequality gives $Y=0$. Extending across compact intervals proves every coefficient is a linear combination of the two modes. [F3, F4, algebra, construct]

## Statement

Let $s$ be a zero-mean grid source and let $\phi$ be the zero-mean solution of $A_h\phi=s$. Let $\widetilde\phi$ be any approximate grid potential, and set $r=s-A_h\widetilde\phi$; then $\bar r=0$. Define
$$\gamma_{N,L}= \max_{\substack{k\in\mathcal K_N\\k\ne0}} \frac{\left(\sum_{a=1}^d h^{-2}\sin^2(2\pi k_a/N)\right)^{1/2}} {4h^{-2}\sum_{a=1}^d\sin^2(\pi k_a/N)} .$$ For the centered field operator $D^0=(D_a^0)_{a=1}^d$, $$\|D^0(\phi-\widetilde\phi)\|_h\le\gamma_{N,L}\|r\|_h,\qquad \gamma_{N,L}\le\frac{h}{2\sin(\pi/N)}\le\frac L4 .$$ For any particle location $x_p$ and charge-to-mass ratio $q_p/m_p$ with $m_p>0$, the force gather using the weights of [[def-periodic-pic-shape-assignment-and-gather]] obeys $$\left|\frac{q_p}{m_p}G_{x_p}\!\left(-D^0\phi+D^0\widetilde\phi\right)\right| \le\frac{|q_p|}{m_p}h^{-d/2}\gamma_{N,L}\|r\|_h .$$
Thus the norm in the force certificate is the actual finite-grid inverse/derivative norm; the explicit $h^{-d/2}$ conversion is retained when passing from grid $L^2$ to a particle gather.

2.1 For a Fourier character $e_k$, direct substitution into the centered difference from [F1] gives $$(D_a^0e_k)_j=\frac{e_k(j+e_a)-e_k(j-e_a)}{2h}=\frac{e^{2\pi i k_a/N}-e^{-2\pi i k_a/N}}{2h}e_k(j)=\frac{i\sin(2\pi k_a/N)}h e_k(j).$$ By [F2], $A_h$ has eigenvalue $\lambda_h(k)>0$ on every nonzero mode, so [F4] implies that $A_h^\dagger r$ has coefficient $\widehat r_k/\lambda_h(k)$ there. Thus the vector multiplier of $D^0A_h^\dagger$ has Euclidean modulus $\left(\sum_a h^{-2}\sin^2(2\pi k_a/N)\right)^{1/2}/\lambda_h(k)$. Parseval's identity for this finite orthogonal basis therefore gives the first bound with the displayed maximum $\gamma_{N,L}$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]
cases.reason: The odd periodic grid has at least three nodes per direction, so the maximum over nonconstant Fourier modes is taken over an inhabited finite set.

## Statement

Let $F$ be the tensor-product NURBS patch of [[def-nurbs-patch-map-and-rational-spline-space]]. Insert a knot $u$ that is new and strictly inside a nonempty span in one coordinate direction. Apply [[alg-single-new-b-spline-knot-insertion]] to every control-net slice in that direction, using homogeneous controls $(w_\alpha P_\alpha,w_\alpha)\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$. Then the updated homogeneous tensor spline is pointwise unchanged, every updated weight is positive, and the rational patch map remains exactly $F$ on $\overline{\widehat\Omega}$.

1.1 Write the homogeneous control array as $\widetilde P_\alpha=(w_\alpha P_\alpha,w_\alpha)$. The tensor spline $\widetilde F(\xi)=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}\widetilde P_\alpha N_\alpha(\xi)$ has first $d$ components $W(\xi)F(\xi)$ and last component $W(\xi)$ by [F3]. Fix the coordinate direction in which $u$ is inserted and fix a multi-index of all other coordinates. Grouping the finite sum over the remaining index writes the corresponding slice as a B-spline curve with controls in $\mathbb R^{d+1}$. By [F2], knot insertion leaves that slice unchanged for every value of the insertion coordinate. Multiplication by the fixed transverse tensor basis function and summation over all transverse indices show that the entire updated homogeneous spline $\widetilde F'$ equals $\widetilde F$ pointwise. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]
cases.reason: Insertion is required inside an existing nonempty knot span, and positive control weights ensure that the homogeneous denominator is not an empty sum.

## Statement

Fix Matérn parameters $d\ge1$, $\nu>0$, $a>0$, $s=\nu+d/2$, an admitted bounded domain $\Omega$, and a mesh-ratio bound $\rho_0>0$. There is $C=C(\Omega,d,\nu,a,\rho_0)$ such that every finite nonempty distinct site set $X\subset\Omega$ with $N\ge2$, $0<q_X\le1$, $0<h_X\le1$, and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X\le\rho_0$ satisfies
$$\kappa_2(K_X)\le C h_X^{-2s}.$$
The one-site case has condition number $1$. This is an exact-arithmetic condition-number estimate for the Gram matrix; it does not bound the error of a floating-point solver.

1.1 Suppose $N\ge2$ and write $q=q_X\le1$. Choose $z_0$ and $R>0$ with $\Omega\subset B(z_0,R)$. The site balls $B(x_i,q)$ are pairwise disjoint and lie in $B(z_0,R+1)$. Their measures are $q^d\lambda(B(0,1))$ by [F2], so finite additivity and the positive finite unit-ball measure give $$Nq^d\lambda(B(0,1))\le(R+1)^d\lambda(B(0,1)),$$ and therefore $N\le C_\Omega q^{-d}$. [F2, A1, given, algebra]
cases.reason: Zero fill distance or zero separation radius is excluded in the multi-site branch, and a zero Gram matrix contradicts normalized kernel positivity.

## Definition

**Inputs.** A nondegenerate interval $I=[a,b]$, degrees $m,n\ge0$, continuous
real target $f$, strictly positive continuous weight $w$, a finite exchange
integer budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, an initial reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{m+n+1})$ satisfying
$a\leq x_0<\cdots<x_{m+n+1}\leq b$, an
exact rational alternation-solver procedure, and an exact weighted-extrema
oracle.

The alternation solver is an explicit input procedure. On a reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{m+n+1})$, it solves the nonlinear equations
$$w(x_i)\bigl(f(x_i)-p(x_i)/q(x_i)\bigr)=(-1)^i\lambda$$
with $p,q$ coprime, $\deg p\le m$, $\deg q\le n$, $q>0$ on $I$, and
$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}=1$. It reports one of: a unique candidate with
defect $d=0$ and its solved level $\lambda$; an exact defective candidate
with its computed $d>0$ and solved level $\lambda$; singular or nonunique
system; no normal solution; or inconclusive. The procedure does not assume
that this nonlinear solve always succeeds.

The weighted-extrema oracle for a returned candidate $r=p/q$ reports one of:

- alternation$(E,Y)$ only when $E=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}$ and $Y$ consists of
  $N_{m,n}(r)+2$ ordered distinct points in $I$ with weighted residuals
  $\sigma(-1)^iE$;
- maximum$(E,x)$ only when $x\in I$, $E=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}$ and
  $|w(x)(f(x)-r(x))|=E$; or
- inconclusive.

**Procedure.** For $k=0,\ldots,B$, call the alternation solver on the current
reference. Return its singular, no-normal-solution, or inconclusive status
unchanged. If it returns a defective candidate, return
defective$(d,N_{m,n}(r))$ immediately; do not apply the normal
$m+n+2$-point count. For a normal candidate $(r,\lambda)$, query the
weighted-extrema oracle. A response alternation$(0,Y)$ or maximum$(0,x)$
returns exact$(r)$, since either certifies zero weighted error. An
alternation response with $E>0$ returns certified$(r,E,Y)$, with optimality supplied by
[[thm-na-weighted-rational-alternation-characterization]]. For maximum$(E,x)$
with $E=|\lambda|$, the current reference itself is an exact global
alternation certificate, so return certified$(r,E,X)$. If $\lambda=0<E$,
return zero-level-no-exchange. If $E>|\lambda|$,
exchange the returned maximum point $x$ for the smallest reference node $x_i$
whose expected sign $\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda)(-1)^i$ matches the sign of
$w(x)(f(x)-r(x))$ and for which replacing $x_i$ by $x$ preserves strict
ordering. If no such index exists, return no-valid-exchange. After $B+1$
unsuccessful iterations, return budget-exhausted.

**Outputs.** The procedure returns an exact minimax certificate, an exact
zero-error candidate, or an explicit defect, singularity, no-solution,
oracle, exchange, or budget status. It claims no existence of a successful
nonlinear solve and no iterative convergence.

## Example

For integers $d\ge3$ and $n\ge2$, let
$$ A=\sum_{j=1}^{n}e_j^{(1)}\otimes e_j^{(2)}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_j^{(d)} \in\mathbb R^{n\times\cdots\times n}. $$

Contracting these Kronecker-delta entries yields $1$ exactly when all mode indices are the same and $0$ otherwise, which is the stated tensor. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{2\times2\times2}$ have nonzero entries $A_{111}=3$, $A_{122}=1$, and $A_{212}=2$, with all other entries zero. Apply sequential TT-SVD with rank cap one at both cuts.

2.1 The second remainder has singular values $3$ and $1$, hence its rank-one truncation discards $\delta_2=1$ and returns the tensor $\widehat A=3e_1\otimes e_1\otimes e_1$. The omitted entries of $A-\widehat A$ are $e_1\otimes e_2\otimes e_2$ and $2e_2\otimes e_1\otimes e_2$, which are orthogonal and have squared norms $1$ and $4$. Therefore $\|A-\widehat A\|_F=\sqrt5=\sqrt{\delta_1^2+\delta_2^2}$, realizing equality in [F3]. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under the discrete stabilizability and detectability hypotheses of [[thm-dare-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], start the exact recurrence of [[alg-finite-budget-structure-preserving-doubling-for-dare]] from $A_0=A$, $G_0=BR^{-1}B^*$, and $H_0=Q$. Then all inverses exist, $G_j,H_j\succeq0$, and $H_j$ converges to the stabilizing DARE solution $X_*$. More quantitatively, there are $q\in(0,1)$, an index $j_0$, and $C>0$ such that
$$\|H_j-X_*\|_{F,W^{-1}}\le Cq^{2^{j+1}}\qquad(j\ge j_0),$$
where $W\succ0$ is a Stein witness constructed from the closed-loop matrix. The envelope $\epsilon_j=Cq^{2^{j+1}}$ obeys $\epsilon_{j+1}=\epsilon_j^2/C$. The constants are conditional on the closed-loop spectral separation and its norm conditioning; no uniform constant depending only on dimension is asserted.

2.1 Let $E_k=X_*-P_k\succeq0$. The Riccati-map difference identity in [F1] gives $E_{k+1}=M^*E_kA_c(P_k).$ Define $\|E\|_{F,W^{-1}}=\|W^{-1/2}EW^{-1/2}\|_F$. By [F5], for $k\ge k_0$, $\|E_{k+1}\|_{F,W^{-1}}\le\|M\|_W\|A_c(P_k)\|_W\|E_k\|_{F,W^{-1}}\le q^2\|E_k\|_{F,W^{-1}}.$ Iteration gives $\|E_k\|_{F,W^{-1}}\le\|E_{k_0}\|_{F,W^{-1}}q^{2(k-k_0)}$. Taking $k=2^j$ and setting $C=\max\{1,\|E_{k_0}\|_{F,W^{-1}}q^{-2k_0}\}$ proves the displayed envelope for all $2^j\ge k_0$. Since $C>0$, direct calculation gives $\epsilon_{j+1}=Cq^{2^{j+2}}=\epsilon_j^2/C$. [F1, F5, step 1.2, algebra, induction] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $T>0$,
$f\in C^1(\mathbb R)$, and $u_0\in\mathrm{BV}_b(\mathbb R)$ in the sense of
[[def-bounded-bv-data-on-line]]. Put
$I=[\operatorname*{ess\,inf}u_0,\operatorname*{ess\,sup}u_0]$. Let
$F\colon\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz, consistent with $f$,
nondecreasing in its first coordinate and nonincreasing in its second on
$I^2$, with coordinate Lipschitz bounds $L_1,L_2$ as in
[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]]. For a family of meshes
$(h_m,\tau_m)$ assume
$$h_m,\tau_m\to0,\qquad \frac{\tau_m}{h_m}(L_1+L_2)\le1,\qquad \frac{\tau_m}{h_m}\ge c_*>0.$$
For each mesh, initialize by cell averages and update with the shared flux $F$.
Let $W_m$ be the piecewise-linear time interpolant and $\mathcal U_m$ the
piecewise-constant state reconstruction. If $u_0\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, assume
Dependent Choice $\mathrm{DC}$ in addition to $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; no DC
assumption is made when $u_0\notin L^1(\mathbb R)$.

Then there is a unique bounded Kruzhkov entropy solution $u$ on
$\mathbb R\times(0,T)$ with initial datum $u_0$, and
$$W_m\longrightarrow u\quad\text{in }C([0,T];L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R)),\qquad \mathcal U_m\longrightarrow u\quad\text{strongly in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T)).$$
For nonintegrable bounded BV data, existence is obtained from the local
finite-volume limit in the proof before local contraction gives uniqueness.
The theorem claims local convergence; global $L^1$ convergence requires
additional uniform tail control. The time-to-space lower bound $c_*$ is retained
from the approved convergence interface, and no system-valued or non-BV
entropy-process conclusion is asserted.

6.1 Every convergent subsequence from step 1.1 has an entropy-solution limit with the same initial data; by [F7] all such limits agree with the unique target from step 5.1 as space-time $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ classes. If the full sequence failed to converge strongly on some compact space-time set, a subsequence would stay at distance at least $\varepsilon>0$ from that target; [F4] would give a further subsequence converging strongly there to an entropy solution, contradicting uniqueness. Therefore $\mathcal U_m\to u$ strongly in local space-time $L^1$. For the uniform-in-time conclusion, Fubini in [F6] turns this space-time equality into equality of the $L^1(K)$ sections for almost every $t$, for each compact interval $K$. The two local-$L^1$ limit maps are continuous, so they agree for every $t$: if their distance were positive at one time, continuity would make it positive on an interval of positive measure. Uniform-in-time local convergence of $W_m$ then follows by the same subsequence contradiction using [F4]. [F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice.

On the unit square split along the diagonal from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, the continuous piecewise-affine pressure with nodal values $0,0,1,0$ at $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$ has negative gradient $q=(0,-1)$ below the diagonal and $q=(-1,0)$ above it. Each cellwise divergence is zero, but the normal flux jumps by magnitude $\sqrt2$ across the diagonal; hence this piecewise field is not in $H(\operatorname{div};D)$ and does not have a locally conservative global flux.

2.1 For $\phi\in C_c^\infty(D)$, integration by parts on the two triangles shows that the distributional divergence of the piecewise field is the nonzero line measure on the diagonal with density $q_1\cdot n-q_2\cdot n=\sqrt2$ in this orientation (the distributional pairing is the negative of the summed outward boundary flux). To see it cannot be an $L^2$ function, choose a nonnegative smooth $\psi$ supported in the open diagonal with positive line integral and a smooth transverse cutoff $\eta$ with $\eta(0)=1$; set $\phi_\varepsilon(y,t)=\psi(y)\eta(t/\varepsilon)$ in tubular coordinates, extended by zero. The surface pairing is the fixed nonzero number $\sqrt2\int\psi$, whereas $\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_{L^2(D)}=O(\varepsilon^{1/2})$. If the distribution were represented by $g\in L^2(D)$, [F2] would give $|\int g\phi_\varepsilon|\le\|g\|_2\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_2\to0$, a contradiction. By [F1] the field is not in H(div). [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, contradiction] ∎
cases.reason: The witness fixes two positive-area triangles covering the square, and its nonzero interior-edge measure cannot be formed on an empty mesh.

## Statement

Assume the affine-element method and all directional entropy/SBP data of [[def-pe04-flux-differencing-sbp-systems]]. Suppose all nodal states remain in $\mathcal A$. Define the discrete entropy and the boundary contribution by
$$E_h(t)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\mathbf1^TH_K\eta(U^K),\qquad \mathcal B_h(t)=\sum_{F\subset\partial\Omega}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}\bigl(v(U_{F,q})^T\widehat F_{n_F}^*-\psi_{n_F}(U_{F,q})\bigr).$$
If $\mathcal B_h(t)\ge0$, then
$$\frac{d}{dt}E_h(t)+\sum_{F\text{ interior}}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}\frac{\alpha_{F,q}}2\lVert[v]_{F,q}\rVert^2+\mathcal B_h(t)=0,$$
so $E_h$ is nonincreasing. Here $\widehat F_{n_F,q}^*$ is the explicitly defined normal flux of [[def-pe04-flux-differencing-sbp-systems]]. On a periodic mesh the boundary contribution cancels with its identified periodic partner. The same semidiscretization conserves the quadrature-weighted total state on a periodic mesh. No fully discrete entropy statement follows.

3.1 Sum the cell entropy rates from step 2.1. By [F5] the two cell contributions at an interior face can be written in one orientation as $-[\psi_n]+[v]^T\widehat F_{n,F,q}^*$. Substitution of the flux definition in [F1] and the directional jump identity [F4] makes this $-\alpha_{F,q}\lVert[v]\rVert^2/2$. The boundary-cell contributions are $-\mathcal B_h$ by definition. Moving these terms to the left gives the asserted identity, and [A1] gives nonincrease. [F1, F4, F5, A1, step 2.1, algebra]

$$E_h(t)=\sum_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\mathbf1^TH_K\eta(U^K),\qquad \mathcal B_h(t)=\sum_{F\subset\partial\Omega}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}\bigl(v(U_{F,q})^T\widehat F_{n_F}^*-\psi_{n_F}(U_{F,q})\bigr).$$
If $\mathcal B_h(t)\ge0$, then
$$\frac{d}{dt}E_h(t)+\sum_{F\text{ interior}}\sum_q\omega_{F,q}\frac{\alpha_{F,q}}2\lVert[v]_{F,q}\rVert^2+\mathcal B_h(t)=0,$$
so $E_h$ is nonincreasing. Here $\widehat F_{n_F,q}^*$ is the explicitly defined normal flux of [[def-pe04-flux-differencing-sbp-systems]]. On a periodic mesh the boundary contribution cancels with its identified periodic partner. The same semidiscretization conserves the quadrature-weighted total state on a periodic mesh. No fully discrete entropy statement follows.

1.1 For a fixed cell and direction write $F_{ij}^{ec}=F_\ell^{ec}(U_i,U_j)$ and $\psi_i=\psi_\ell(U_i)$. Symmetry of $F_\ell^{ec}$ from [F4] gives $2\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}v_i^TF_{ij}^{ec}=\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}(v_i-v_j)^TF_{ij}^{ec}+\sum_{i,j}(Q_{ij}+Q_{ji})v_j^TF_{ij}^{ec}$. By [F4] the first sum is $\sum_{i,j}Q_{ij}(\psi_i-\psi_j)=-\sum_j\psi_j(Q^T\mathbf1)_j=-\sum_F\sum_q\omega_{F,q}\psi_{n_F}(U_{F,q})$, since $Q\mathbf1=0$ and $Q^T\mathbf1=(Q+Q^T)\mathbf1$ by [F2]. The second sum is $\sum_F\sum_q\omega_{F,q}v(U_{F,q})^TF_{n_F}(U_{F,q})$ by [F2], diagonal face selection, and consistency from [F4]. Summing directions and the potential identity in [F3] proves the volume entropy boundary identity. [F2, F3, F4, algebra]
